sections.body:
**Rnnwtt** ​(*renenutet*) — ‌The Harvest, ‌the ​Nursing Cobra ​· ​The nursing ​snake — ​belongs ‌to the ​Egyptian ​tradition, where ‌it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Nursing, ‌Harvest". ​The name ​means ​"The nursing ​snake"[^1].

**Rnnwtt** ​— ‌Renenutet — ​is ‌the harvest ​as maternity: ‌the ​cobra who ‌coils ​in the ‌last standing ​sheaf ​and nurses ‌the grain ‌to ‌ripeness. Every ​Egyptian ​granary was ‌her temple ​in ​miniature; every ‌nurse ​suckling a ​child repeated ‌her ​oldest work. ‌She is ​the ​goddess in ​whom ​food and ‌motherhood are ‌the ​same fact.[^2]

‌PuniCodex ​records the ​canonical scholarly ‌spelling ‌**Rnnwtt** and ‌serves its ‌temple ​at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/renenutet/). ​The displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent ‌— a ​description ​computed from ​the displayed ‌form ​itself. The ​plain ​ASCII form ‌*renenutet* contains ​the ‌same letters: ​no recovered ‌diacritics ​or special ‌encoding ‌is claimed. ​The work ​here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Hieroglyphs ​as **𓂋𓈖𓈖𓅱𓏏𓏏𓆗**. ​Etymologically ​it means ​"The nursing ​snake"[^1].

‌The canonical ​spelling ​**Rnnwtt** matches ‌the conventional ​scholarly ‌romanization. The ​plain ‌ASCII form ​*renenutet* contains ​the ​same letters, ​so ​no lost ‌diacritics or ​encoding ‌transition is ​claimed. ‌The editorial ​work is ‌to ​fix one ‌reviewed ​reference spelling, ​preserve capitalization ‌and ‌provenance, and ‌keep ​the original ​evidence visible. ‌The ​displayed form ​is ‌ASCII-equivalent — ​a description ​computed ‌from the ​displayed ‌form itself.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- **r** ​→ ‌**R** — ‌Same, capitalized
- ​**e** ‌→ **n** ​— ​Special phonetic ‌character
- **n** ‌→ ‌**n** — ‌Same
- ​**e** → ‌**w** — ​Special ​phonetic character
- ​**n** ‌→ **t** ​— Special ​phonetic ​character
- **u** ‌→ ​**t** — ​Special phonetic ​character
- ‌**t** → ​**—** ‌— Dropped: ​vowel not ‌written
- ​**e** → ‌**—** ‌— Dropped: ​vowel not ​written
- ​**t** → ​**—** ‌— Dropped: ‌vowel not ​written

sections.body:
**Rnnwtt** ​— Renenutet ‌— ‌is ​the harvest ​as ​maternity: ​the cobra ​who ‌coils in ​the ​last ‌standing sheaf ​and ‌nurses ​the grain ‌to ​ripeness. Every ​Egyptian ​granary ​was her ​temple ‌in ​miniature; every ‌nurse ​suckling a ‌child ​repeated ‌her oldest ​work. ‌She ​is the ​goddess ‌in whom ‌food ‌and ​motherhood are ​the ‌same ​fact.[^1]

### The ​Harvest ‌Cobra

A ​rearing ​cobra ‌crowned with ​the ‌harvest’s ​plumes; the ​last ​sheaf of ​the ‌field ‌is her ​shrine.

### ‌Lady ​of the ​Granary

‌Every storehouse ‌and ‌threshing ‌floor fell ​under ‌her ​protection — ​and ​her audit.

### ‌The ​Nursing ​Goddess

Her ​name ‌means ​“she who ​nurses”; ​the pharaoh ‌himself ​was ‌her nursling.

### ​Goddess ‌of ​the Vineyard

‌Wine-presses ‌and wine-jars ​carried ​her ​name; the ​vintage ‌was ‌her second ​harvest.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Renenutet’s mythology ​is the theology ‌of food security ‌in a subsistence ​economy: the goddess ​who turns sunlight ​into grain and ​grain into children’s ​milk. She has ‌no great narrative ​cycle because she ​needed none — ‌every harvest was ​her epiphany, every ‌famine her absence, ​every granary her ‌chapel.[^1]

### The Cobra ​in the Last ​Sheaf (Harvest Theology)

​Egyptian reapers left ​the last sheaf ​standing and addressed ‌it as Renenutet: ​the goddess still ‌resident in the ​field. To cut ‌it was to ​release her into ‌the granary for ​the year’s safekeeping. ‌The custom — ​attested from the ​Old Kingdom harvest ‌scenes onward — ‌made every field’s ‌end a small ​theological drama.[^2]

### Mother ​of the Vineyard ‌(Fayum & Dendera)

​In the Fayum ​and at Dendera ‌she presided over ​the wine-press as ​over the threshing-floor; ‌the wine-jar docket ​‘Renenutet’s portion’ marked ‌the divine tithe ​of the vintage. ​With Sobek as ​her consort in ​the Fayum she ‌mothered the crop-cycle ‌whole — grain, ​grape, and the ‌flood that feeds ​both.

### Nurse of ​the King (Royal ‌Nurture)

The king’s ‌titulary calls him ‌‘the nursling of ‌Renenutet’: the harvest ​feeds the state ‌as the breast ​feeds the child, ​and both are ​her body. Royal ‌birth-scenes show her ​cobra rearing behind ​the throne of ​the nursing mother, ‌transferring the goddess’ ​own milk into ​the legitimate succession.

### ​Thermouthis (Greco-Roman Age)

‌Under the Ptolemies ​she was worshipped ‌as Thermouthis — ​‘the harvest-serpent’ in ‌Greek dress — ​with a cult ‌that joined her ‌to Isis the ​nurse. The equation ​made her an ​international goddess of ​provisioning, and her ‌images spread with ‌the grain trade ​she embodied.
